JMPR: Metalaxyl (sum of enantiomers)
EU: Reg. 396/2005 (implementing MRL review): Metalaxyl and metalaxyl-M (metalaxyl including other mixtures of constituent isomers including metalaxyl-M (sum of isomers))
efsa_comments:
JMPR meeting assessed seven metabolism studies for primary crops on grapes (2 studies), lettuce (2 studies) and potato (3 studies) conducted with metalaxyl and metalaxyl-M. In grapes and potato tubers, metalaxyl represented the major compound (64% of TRR and 57% of TRR, respectively) while M8 accounted 20% of TRR in grapes and 4 of TRR in potato tubers. In lettuce, M8 was the main compound accounting up to 61% of TRR, mainly conjugated form), while metalaxyl represented 19% of TRR.
Since M8 was not analysed in the residue trials, JMPR derived conversion factors to recalculate the results of metalaxyl to the residue definition for risk assessment (CF 11 for leafy crops and 1.3 for fruits and non-leafy vegetables) No conversion factor required for bulb, root and tuber crops and for crops where no residues are expected to be found. Rotational crops metabolism studies were conducted with metalaxyl and metalaxyl-M in several crops covering all crops group of leafy, roots and cereals.
Various metabolites were found, SYN546555 a breakdown compound of M8 was major in wheat hay (40% TRR), M1 (20% sugar beet root), M5 (up to 45% TRR in wheat hay), M8 in wheat stalk (33% TRR), mature lettuce (up 21% TRR), radish leaves (19% TRR) and wheat forage (40% TRR). Metalaxyl was found > 10% only in radish leaves at 120-day PBI. Except SYN546555, all the other metabolites found in rotational crops were found in primary crops. EU RA RD for plants was limited to metalaxyl (sum of enantiomers).
It is noted that the primary metabolism studies evaluated in EU were not all the same (additional studies on tobacco, tomatoes and wheat considered). In the ongoing assessment on the renewal of the approval (AIR peer review), it was decided to exclude M8 from the RD RA due to its low occurrence levels observed in GAP-compliant field trials on grapes and tomatoes.
In the AIR peer review of metalaxyl-M, only a DEREK analysis was available for M8, but as it is structurally very related to CGA 108906 and SYN546520, for which several studies were available, it was considered toxicologically covered.
The available livestock metabolism shows that metalaxyl is rapidly metabolised to various components free and conjugates with M3 being the major residue in milk and muscle (70% TRR in milk and 30% hen muscle), M6 (max 31% TRR tissues) M8 (max 34% TRR in kidney), M1 and M7 in goat muscle (max 14% TRR) and fat (40% of TRR). Metalaxyl was recovered only in eggs for 6% TRR. Although no metabolism studies with metalaxyl-M were available is not expected to lead to formation of different compounds.
Analytical methods for animal products were mainly based on common moiety methods; the methods were not sufficiently validated for the metabolites. JMPR did not propose CXL for animal commodities, because no validated analytical methods are available that include the determination of metabolites. In the EU assessment, the EU MRLs for animal products were tentatively set, requesting analytical methods for enforcement for animal products.
This data gap was not addressed in the framework of the confirmatory data assessment, and therefore, EFSA suggested further risk management considerations for animal products (EFSA, 2021i).

JMPR: Methoprene
EU: Reg. 396/2005: Methoprene No EU review or EU MRL review
efsa_comments:
At EU level, no risk assessment residue definitions have been set since methoprene was never assessed for its residue behaviour. Considering the log Pow, the modification of the residue definition, including the label (F) for fat-soluble substances should be considered in the EU. The residue definition of JMPR was based on metabolism studies in wheat (post-harvest treatment), alfalfa and rice (both foliar application).
No specific metabolism studies are available for oilseeds (post-harvest treatment).

JMPR: Clofentezine
EU: Peer review (EFSA, 2021e): Clofentezine and 2-CBN. Applicable only to fruit crops following foliar treatment. The residue definition for risk assessment for other crop groups and for processed commodities remains open.
efsa_comments:
EU RD for plants: As regards the RD RA for plant products, the peer review noted that the way the risk assessment residue definition should be expressed is pending on further clarification on the toxicological profile of metabolite 2-CBN since its aneugenicity assessment and general toxicity are outstanding. As the process on renewal of the approval is still ongoing, the final decision on the residue definitions has not yet been taken by risk managers.
JMPR RD for plants: JMPR assessed a new metabolism study following foliar treatment of lettuce, where parent compound was the only residue identified.

JMPR: Fenpyroximate
EU: Reg. 396/2005 (implementing MRL review): Fenpyroximate Peer review (EFSA, 2013l): Fenpyroximate
efsa_comments:
For plant products, the EU and JMPR RDs (RA and enforcement) for the crops under assessment are identical. The residue definitions for animal products derived by JMPR and at EU level are not fully compatible: The JMPR enforcement RD for animal products is apparently more comprehensive covering for all matrices the parent compound and the main metabolite M-3, while the EU RD contains only the marker substances, i.e.
M-3 for liver and kidney of ruminants, equines and other farmed terrestrial mammals and parent compound for other matrices. The RDs for RA for animal products are also different with respect to R-UL1 which is included only in the JMPR RD and the Z-isomers of Fen-OH and M-3 which are included only in the EU RD.

JMPR: Sum of fipronil and 5-amino-3-cyano-1-(2,6-dichloro-4-trifluoro methylphenyl)-4-trifluoromethylsulfonyl pyrazole (MB46136) expressed in terms of fipronil
EU: Reg. 396/2005: Fipronil (Sum fipronil + sulfone metabolite (MB46136) expressed as fipronil) MRL review (EFSA, 2012e) and peer review EFSA (2006c): Sum of fipronil and sulfone metabolite (MB 46136) expressed as fipronil
efsa_comments:
Fipronil sulfone metabolite (MB46136) Fipronil desulfinyl metabolite (MB46513) Fipronil sulfide metabolite (MB45950) The enforcement residue definitions derived by the JMPR and the EU peer review/MRL review are comparable. The risk assessment residue definition derived by the JMPR is wider than the EU risk assessment residue definition. It includes the sum of fipronil, the desulfinyl metabolite (MB46513), the sulfone metabolite (MB46136) and the sulfide metabolite (MB45950).
New metabolism studies, investigating the metabolic pathway of fipronil following foliar treatments were evaluated by the JMPR 2021 (cabbage potato, rice, cotton, sunflower) which have not been available for the EU assessments. These studies, however, were not the reason to amend the residue definition for risk assessment as derived by the JMPR in 2002. The studies confirmed the presence of photometabolite of fipronil (desulfinyl metabolite (MB46513)) following foliar treatment.
The sulfide metabolite (MB45950), also included in the risk assessment residue definitions, was present in rice straw (9.3–16.8%) following seed/foliar treatment, but generally not detected or present at low levels in other commodities. The sulfide metabolite (MB45950) was present also in goat matrices (up to 12% TRR).
Overall, the JMPR concluded that metabolites MB46513 and MB45950 could make a significant contribution to the overall consumer exposure when compared with estimates for the sum of fipronil and fipronil-sulfone and therefore included these compounds in the risk assessment residue definition. The EU pesticides peer review derived the risk assessment and enforcement residue definitions for the representative use, i.e.
seed treatment; the photodegradation product of fipronil-desulfinyl metabolite (MB46513) was not included in the residue definitions as unlikely to occur in seed treatments or soil incorporation. However, because of concern that the desulfinyl metabolite forms as a result of photodegradation, it was proposed that treated seed must be kept in the dark prior to use. The MRL review confirmed the residue definitions derived by the EU pesticides peer review.
The risk assessment residue definition derived by the JMPR is adequate to account for the potential metabolites of fipronil in plant commodities (from seed/soil and foliar applications) and in animal matrices. The exposure assessment performed according to this residue definition is expected to be protective for consumers. The JMPR also evaluated hydrolysis studies submitted to investigate the effect of processing on the nature of fipronil, MB46136 and MB46153.
Fipronil under sterilisation conditions slightly degraded for 5.5% AR to fipronil-amide (toxicity covered by fipronil). Fipronil sulfone (MB46136) also degraded under sterilisation conditions only and for 8.4% AR to RPA105320 (fipronil-sulfone-amide). Fipronil-desulfinyl was the most unstable and under sterilisation conditions formed two major degradation products: MB46400 (10.5% AR) and fipronil-carboxamide (25.9% AR; RPA105048).
For the estimation of consumer exposure to these degradation products the JMPR proposed to apply the TTC (Cramer Class III threshold of 1.5 μg/kg bw per day).

JMPR: Prothioconazole-desthio
EU: Reg. 396/2005 (implementing MRL review): Prothioconazole-desthio (sum of isomers) Peer review (EFSA, 2007): Prothioconazole-desthio (sum of isomers)
efsa_comments:
In the framework of the renewal of the approval of prothioconazole, the Pesticides Peer Review Teleconference 25 (28–29 September 2020) confirmed the RD enforcement for plant and animal products (prothioconazole-desthio (M04) (sum of isomers)); New provisional RD for RA were proposed in this meeting for plants: Sum of prothioconazole-desthio (M04) and prothioconazole-desthio-3-hydroxy (M14), prothioconazole-desthio-4-hydroxy (M15), prothioconazole-desthio-5-hydroxy (M16), prothioconazole-desthio-6-hydroxy (M17) and prothioconazole-desthio-alpha-hydroxy (M18) and their conjugates expressed as prothioconazole-desthio.
The proposed RD are provision, pending submission of genotoxicity data on M15 and M17. (CF of 1 for root, tuber and pulses, and oilseed commodities and CF of 3 for cereal straw were proposed).
New provisional RD for RA for animal products: Sum of prothioconazole-desthio (M04) free and conjugated, prothioconazole-desthio-3-hydroxy (M14), prothioconazole-desthio-4-hydroxy (M15), prothioconazole-desthio-3,4-dihydroxy (M33), prothioconazole-desthio-4,5-dihydroxy (M35), free and their conjugates expressed as prothioconazole-desthio equiv.
The proposed RD is considered as provisional pending the submission of toxicity data to address the genotoxic potential and the general toxicity of M15, M33 and M35. (Proposed CF: 2 for liver, 4 for kidney based on the goat metabolism, no CF for milk, muscle and fat since the residue levels in these matrices are expected to be negligible). In addition, RD for TDMs were proposed for plant and animal products (RD RA):
  * • TA and TLA, since these compounds share the same toxicity,
  * • TAA,
  * • 1,2,4-triazole
JMPR did not establish residue definitions for risk assessment covering the TDMs. For prothioconazole, in principle, the conclusions from the EU pesticides peer review on the risk assessment for the triazole derivative metabolites (TDMs) in the light of confirmatory data would also apply on the need to consider TDMs in the residue definitions.
The EU residue definition for risk assessment for plants is more comprehensive, covering all the metabolites containing the 2-(1-chlorocyclopropyl)-3-(2-chlorophenyl)-2-hydroxypropyl-2H-1,2,4-triazole moiety; conversion factors for enforcement to risk assessment were derived: 2 for cereal grain, pulses and oilseeds, leafy vegetables and root and tuber vegetables; 3 for cereal straw. Since for fruit crops metabolism data are not available, a generic conversion factor for risk assessment is not available.
For animal commodities, the EU and JMPR risk assessment residue definitions are different. From the metabolism studies presented in the 2008 JMPR report, it seems that some of the major metabolites identified in animal commodities are not covered by the JMPR residue definition. The JMPR RA residue definition reflects only those metabolites which were analysed in the cow-feeding study.
The potential inclusion of glucuronide conjugate in the enforcement residue definition for all livestock matrices was recommended by the MRL review in case the EU livestock DB is increasing. From livestock metabolism studies, conversion factors from enforcement to risk assessment were derived as 2 for liver and 9 for kidney and 1 for other matrices. As the renewal process is still ongoing, further modifications of the residue definitions might be proposed in the EU.

EU: Reg. 396/2005: Sulfoxaflor The residue is not fat soluble
efsa_comments:
The residue definitions for enforcement set by JMPR and at EU level are substantially identical, since the ISO common name sulfoxaflor covers the two diastereomeric pairs of enantiomers of sulfoxaflor. At EU level, the residue definition for risk assessment in plant and animal commodities is more comprehensive and includes the metabolite X11719474.
X11719474 is a plant and soil metabolite, which has shown to be preferentially taken up by the roots of the plants and to be present (> LOQ) in the leafy parts of the crops in rotation crops, particularly in feed items. The EU pesticide peer review considered metabolite X11719474 to be quantitatively relevant in primary and rotational crops (EFSA, 2014j). However, its inclusion in the residue definition for risk assessment of plant and animal products is provisional.
Lacking toxicological data on the metabolite, currently, exposure assessments are performed, assuming that this metabolite is as toxic as the parent compound. The EU pesticides peer review agreed that if metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for the risk assessment should be revised to parent sulfoxaflor only.

EU: Peer review (EFSA, 2014j): Sum of parent sulfoxaflor and metabolite X11719474, expressed as sulfoxaflor. If metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for risk assessment will become parent sulfoxaflor only
efsa_comments:
The residue definitions for enforcement set by JMPR and at EU level are substantially identical, since the ISO common name sulfoxaflor covers the two diastereomeric pairs of enantiomers of sulfoxaflor. At EU level, the residue definition for risk assessment in plant and animal commodities is more comprehensive and includes the metabolite X11719474.
X11719474 is a plant and soil metabolite, which has shown to be preferentially taken up by the roots of the plants and to be present (> LOQ) in the leafy parts of the crops in rotation crops, particularly in feed items. The EU pesticide peer review considered metabolite X11719474 to be quantitatively relevant in primary and rotational crops (EFSA, 2014j). However, its inclusion in the residue definition for risk assessment of plant and animal products is provisional.
Lacking toxicological data on the metabolite, currently, exposure assessments are performed, assuming that this metabolite is as toxic as the parent compound. The EU pesticides peer review agreed that if metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for the risk assessment should be revised to parent sulfoxaflor only.

JMPR: Pydiflumetofen The residue is fat soluble
EU: Reg. 396/2005: No specific MRLs established (default MRL according to Art. 18(1)(b) Peer review proposal (EFSA, 2019g): Pydiflumetofen The residue is fat soluble
efsa_comments:
As the EU approval process is still ongoing, a final decision on the residue definitions has not yet been taken. Currently, the default residue definitions (Art. 18(1)(b)) are applicable for enforcement. The residue definitions proposed in the EFSA conclusion are comparable with the Codex residue definitions except for animal products (risk assessment).
For animal products (all matrices), a provisional residue definition for risk assessment was proposed, which covers the parent compound and 2,4,6-TCP. However, for 2,4,6-TPC, additional toxicological data were requested. As reported by the RMS, additional data on 2,4,6-TPC were assessed in a revised DAR which may be sufficient to derive a definitive RD for RA for animal products.
The JMPR residue definition for animal products (risk assessment) for mammalian liver and kidney is wider than the proposed provisional EU RD. The EU residue definitions for primary crops were proposed to be applied also to rotational crops. Pydiflumetofen is a very persistent compound (DT50 = 8,540 days EU value), the accumulation of residue and consequently the uptake from the soil cannot be neglected (see also the general comment from the MRL assessment).

JMPR: Flutianil
EU: Reg. 396/2005: Flutianil Peer review (EFSA, 2014n): Flutianil (fruits and leafy crops only)
efsa_comments:
The same metabolism studies were assessed by JMPR and EU. In the four metabolism studies in fruits (grapes, apples, cucumbers) and leafy (lettuce) flutianil was the major compound among all studies. Metabolites including OC 56635 also occurred in relevant amounts (> 10% of TRRs) but mainly in the non-edible part of the crops.
JMPR RD for plants: For risk assessment JMPR proposed a wider residue definition including also OC 56635) in RA RD for plant, considering the result from the grape trials were OC 56635 found > 0.01 mg/kg and the information from the rotational metabolism studies where this metabolite was shown to be the major one (83% of TRR) which was found to be highly persistent. EU RD for plants: Flutianil only, with additional data required for rotational crops.
The RMS informed EFSA that studies on rotational crops have been provided in the framework of the recent MRL application (EFSA, 2021g); a review of the current residue definition as regards the possible inclusion of metabolite OC 56635 should be considered. JMPR RD for animal commodities: A goat metabolism studies over dosed study (10 ppm for 5 days) showed flutianil metabolised into numerous compounds from 10% up 82% of TRRs but not identified. No metabolism studies on poultry were available.
Since the max dietary burden from current use was 0.06 mg/kg and no metabolism data in animal was available for OC 56635, JMPR considered not possible to derive a RA RD for animals. EU RD for animal commodities: No metabolism studies were triggered by the previous EU assessment (peer review and import tolerance application), therefore no RA-RD for animal was proposed. For monitoring, JMPR and EU considered flutianil was the best marker in plant and animals.
For the commodities for which Codex MRL proposals were derived by JMPR in 2019, the difference of residue definitions for risk assessment of plants is of low relevance since these Codex MRLs under discussion refer to permanent crops only.

JMPR: Sum of pyrasulfotole and desmethyl-pyrasulfotole, expressed as pyrasulfotole. The residue is not fat soluble
EU: Reg. 396/2005: Pyrasulfotole The residue is not fat soluble
efsa_comments:
The active substance has never been assessed at EU level. The EU residue definitions for enforcement was established in 2008, when the a.s. was included in Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 (MRLs above the LOQ set for oats, liver and kidney of bovine). The proposed residue definitions are based on metabolism studies with wheat, rotational crops and livestock.
In cereals, pyrasulfotole was extensively metabolised and not detected in grains; pyrasulfotole-benzoic acid (MTFM-BA) was the main compound (24–98% TRR) in all wheat matrices (forage, hay, straw and grains). Glucose conjugates of desmethyl-pyrasulfotole were identified in wheat forage, hay and straw; desmethyl-pyrasulfotole was predominant residue in field trials.
MTFM-BA was identified as the only metabolite in rotational crops > 0.01 mg/kg (it is a common soil metabolite of isoxaflutole, but DT50 for this metabolite varied between studies). It is noted that the residue definition in plant commodities shall be restricted to cereals only. In livestock metabolism, pyrasulfotole was the predominant compound in animal matrices, milk and eggs; desmethyl- pyrasulfotole was the major metabolite identified in milk (12% TRR).
Livestock feeding studies were available in lactating cows (pyrasulfotole) and laying hens (MTFM-BA). On the basis that MTFM-BA is a common metabolite with isoxaflutole and that it is a (minor) rat metabolite and of no toxicological concern according to toxicity studies, it was not included in the residue definitions for plant and animal matrices. The metabolite is also the main compound the livestock is exposed to.
Validated analytical enforcement methods are available to control residues of pyrasulfotole, desmethyl-pyrasulfotole (free and conjugated) and MTFM-BA in plant and animal matrices. The method involves hydrolysis step to release conjugates. The storage stability of desmethyl-pyrasulfotole is limited to 3 months in high water content commodities (relevant for forage) and dry feed.
